overview: This sortie is about recognizing a landing abnormality early enough to wave off, reconfigure, or buy time for a safer recovery before you make it worse. Be ready to brief hard-landing causes, methodical gear and flap abnormal handling, and the emergency-orbit pattern logic that keeps the aircraft predictable while you troubleshoot.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Hard landings usually come from a landing that was already unstable before the wheels ever touched. The goal in this event is to recognize the bad picture early enough to wave off instead of trying to rescue it in the flare.

children.text: High flare: starting the flare too early or with too much pitch can leave you out of energy high above the runway, followed by a drop-in or a nose-gear-first correction.
Late or rapid flare: misjudged height or high sink rate drives an abrupt pull that can produce a hard touchdown or approach-to-stall right over the runway.
Low airspeed or low power on final is the classic trap. Below 110 KIAS, especially with landing flaps and low power, sink rate builds fast and engine spool-up may not save a delayed waveoff.
Maximum landing weight is 6900 pounds, maximum ramp weight is 6950 pounds, and the max zero-fuel weight is 5850 pounds.
Maximum touchdown rate is 600 FPM with mains serviced to 185 +/- 5 PSI and 780 FPM with mains serviced to 225 +/- 5 PSI.
High temperature and high pressure altitude matter because engine response is slower and a late waveoff becomes less recoverable.
Shift your visual focus to the runway end, keep the flare smooth, and do not try to fix a bad approach once you are already over the runway with no energy margin left.
Wave off early if the approach is high, low, unstable, or no longer comfortable. A delayed waveoff is how a routine recovery becomes a structural-damage event.
If you do have a hard landing, do not raise the gear. Treat the aircraft like it may already be structurally compromised.

items.text: Gear emergencies are really a controllability-and-indication problem first, not a checklist race. The point of the pattern work is to buy time, preserve fuel margin, and confirm what the gear is actually doing before you commit to a landing configuration.

children.text: If the gear does not indicate fully up or fully down as commanded, get the aircraft stable, remain below 150 KIAS, and work the landing-gear malfunction logic methodically.
Use lamp test, hydraulic-pressure check, circuit-breaker status, and gear-handle cycling to sort out whether you have an indication problem, an extension problem, or a true unsafe-gear configuration.
If another aircraft, tower, or RDO can inspect the gear visually, use that help. External confirmation is often safer than guessing from one cockpit indication.
Hydraulic pressure below about 1800 PSI pushes you toward emergency extension logic instead of continued normal troubleshooting.
If the LDGGR CONT circuit breaker is out, you lose more than lights: landing and taxi lights, AOA indexers, ground-idle logic, and nosewheel steering can all be affected.
Any safe gear-down indication you can trust should shift the plan toward landing as soon as practical instead of endlessly cycling the system.
Emergency extension is a one-way decision for the gear and flap picture. Once you pull the handle, retraction is no longer available.
If gear indications remain unsafe, brief the landing around the actual gear you believe is available and treat anything not fully extended as retracted.
Blown-tire or tire-failure cases are still directional-control emergencies. Land on the side of the runway that favors the good tire when able, and do not taxi with a flat tire.

items.text: Flap failures are usually handled as controllability problems, not as a challenge to keep moving switches. Your job is to stabilize the asymmetry, preserve control authority, and set up the simplest landing profile available.

children.text: A split-flap or asymmetric-flap condition can create roll and yaw during flap movement because the two sides are no longer producing the same lift and drag.
If asymmetry shows up, move the flap handle only enough to minimize or eliminate the asymmetry, then stop moving it.
If needed, get visual confirmation of flap position from another aircraft or a ground observer rather than guessing.
Do not extend the speed brake with asymmetric flaps.
Adjust airspeed to maintain control and reduce pilot workload rather than fixating on one nominal pattern number.
Plan a straight-in approach so you are not adding more turning or configuration changes than necessary.

items.text: The emergency orbit pattern is a holding pattern over the field that buys you time and predictable spacing when a landing emergency or runway change makes the normal pattern a bad place to troubleshoot.

children.text: Treat it as a racetrack aligned with the active runway, flown in the normal traffic-flow direction, at the locally briefed orbit altitude.
Standard baseline picture is 120 KIAS with gear down and flaps up unless the emergency itself requires something different.
Once established, keep the aircraft predictable, make the required orbit calls, and use the extra time to work the problem rather than inventing new pattern geometry.
Confirm the current local orbit altitude, entry, and exit rules from the day-of SOP or controlling agency rather than memorizing one field's named pattern.
Do not descend, re-enter the normal pattern, or depart the orbit without the controlling agency's coordination unless a greater emergency requires it.
The orbit pattern is there to create margin. If fuel, controllability, or runway suitability is becoming the bigger emergency, stop troubleshooting and transition to the safer recovery option.
Do not treat the orbit pattern like a holding place for endless troubleshooting. If fuel state, aircraft control, or runway suitability is deteriorating, leave the orbit in the safest available way.
Stay predictable for other traffic. Emergency margin is lost quickly when the orbit turns into improvised geometry or unbriefed altitude changes.
If the emergency itself requires something other than the baseline 120-KIAS, gear-down, flaps-up picture, brief that change early so the orbit remains a deliberate plan rather than a surprise.

items.text: Treat this as a cumulative critical-action EP review where recognition and branch logic matter as much as the first memory items. If the instructor jumps from a landing abnormal to an engine or ground emergency, you should not have to rebuild the whole picture from scratch.

children.text: Be ready for the core ground and departure set: Fire on the Ground, Emergency Engine Shutdown on the Ground, Emergency Ground Egress, Abort Takeoff, Aircraft Departs Prepared Surface, and Engine Failure Immediately After Takeoff.
Be ready for the airborne set: Engine Failure During Flight, Immediate Air-Start, PMU NORM Air-Start, PMU OFF Air-Start, and Uncommanded Power Changes/LOP.
Use the dedicated EP and N/W/C references for verbatim retention. This section is about keeping the follow-on landing, PEL, forced-landing, and ejection decisions connected to the checklist.
Lead with the cue, then the immediate action, then the next safe outcome.
Do not separate the EP from its notes, warnings, and cautions; the caution is often the reason one branch is safer than another.
If you can recite the checklist but cannot explain when you would land, orbit, PEL, or eject, the event will still feel unfinished.

studyNotes.summary: Prevent the hard landing early, manage gear or flap abnormalities methodically, and use the orbit pattern only to buy time for a safer landing answer.
